reviews.scope: stating the geometric justification for copying angles and bisecting angles
reviews.reason: Stating the theoretical basis for straightedge-and-compass angle copying and bisection is an explicit criterion, and both constructions rely on proving auxiliary triangles congruent via Side-Side-Side (SSS).

reviews.scope: understanding equal angles and the definition of an angle bisector
reviews.reason: Constructing an angle equal to a given angle and bisecting an angle with straightedge and compass requires knowing what angle equality and an angle bisector mean.

reviews.scope: proving that a point on an angle bisector is equidistant from the sides
reviews.reason: Proving the angle bisector property is an explicit criterion and relies on showing two right triangles share a hypotenuse and have two pairs of equal angles via AAS or ASA.

reviews.scope: defining distance from a point on the bisector to each side of the angle
reviews.reason: The angle bisector property equates the distances from a point to the two sides of an angle, requiring the concept that point-to-line distance is the perpendicular segment length.

reviews.scope: distinguishing the angle bisector criterion from the angle bisector property
reviews.reason: The mastery criteria explicitly require distinguishing the angle bisector criterion from its converse property, which necessitates knowing the angle bisector property.

reviews.scope: proving the angle bisector criterion via right triangle congruence
reviews.reason: Proving that an interior point equidistant from two sides of an angle lies on the bisector involves two right triangles with a shared hypotenuse and equal legs, requiring HL.

reviews.scope: selecting congruence criteria and writing complete proofs after adding auxiliary lines
reviews.reason: Completing deductive proofs that involve auxiliary constructions directly requires choosing appropriate triangle congruence criteria and writing formal geometric proofs.

reviews.scope: applying the median-doubling auxiliary construction in triangle congruence proofs
reviews.reason: Doubling a triangle median is an explicitly named construction in this node, requiring the definition of a median and the fact that it bisects the opposite side.

reviews.scope: identifying line-symmetric figures, axes of symmetry, and corresponding points
reviews.reason: Distinguishing single line-symmetric figures from pairs of figures in reflection symmetry and finding axes of symmetry builds directly on the foundational concept of line symmetry.

reviews.scope: understanding complete coincidence of two figures and corresponding points
reviews.reason: Knowing that congruent figures coincide completely and have corresponding vertices provides a helpful analogy for two figures coinciding under folding across an axis of symmetry.
reviews.counterexample: A student can understand line symmetry and reflection symmetry directly through folding along a line without using formal triangle congruence notation.

reviews.scope: understanding axes of symmetry and symmetric points when stating reflection properties
reviews.reason: Stating and applying the properties of reflection symmetry requires first knowing the definitions of reflection symmetry, symmetric points, and the axis of symmetry.

reviews.scope: understanding that the axis of symmetry is perpendicular to the segment joining symmetric points
reviews.reason: A core property of reflection symmetry is that the axis of symmetry is perpendicular to the segment connecting symmetric points, requiring the concept of perpendicular lines.

reviews.scope: understanding that reflected figures have equal corresponding segments and angles
reviews.reason: Familiarity with corresponding sides and angles of congruent triangles helps students understand why reflected figures are congruent, though the core new property focuses on perpendicular bisection.
reviews.counterexample: One can determine the axis of symmetry as the perpendicular bisector of symmetric points directly from folding without invoking triangle congruence properties.

reviews.scope: motivating the perpendicular bisector as the axis of symmetry of a segment
reviews.reason: Reflection symmetry provides an intuitive motivation for perpendicular bisectors, but the equidistant property and converse criterion can be defined and proved purely via perpendicularity, midpoints, and triangle congruence.
reviews.counterexample: Define a perpendicular bisector directly from perpendicularity at a segment midpoint and prove its property and criterion via SAS and HL or SSS triangle congruence without reflection symmetry.

reviews.scope: proving the perpendicular bisector theorem and converse and writing segment equality proofs
reviews.reason: Establishing both the property and converse criterion of a perpendicular bisector and applying them in deductive proofs requires selecting triangle congruence criteria and writing formal proofs.

reviews.scope: understanding the midpoint condition in the definition of a perpendicular bisector
reviews.reason: A perpendicular bisector passes through the midpoint of a segment and divides it into two equal parts, which requires the concept and property of a segment midpoint.

reviews.scope: justifying the straightedge-and-compass construction of a perpendicular bisector
reviews.reason: Stating the theoretical basis for constructing a perpendicular bisector is an explicit criterion and relies on the criterion that points equidistant from endpoints lie on the perpendicular bisector.

reviews.scope: constructing the reflection of a point across a given line
reviews.reason: Constructing the symmetric point of a given vertex across a line requires using the property that the axis of symmetry perpendicularly bisects the segment joining symmetric points.

reviews.scope: reflecting polygons by finding symmetric vertices and connecting them
reviews.reason: Drawing reflected figures across general lines introduces the vertex-by-vertex strategy, but coordinate-plane reflections can be found algebraically by negating coordinates and plotting points without geometric perpendicular constructions.
reviews.counterexample: To reflect a polygon across the x-axis or y-axis, negate the y-coordinates or x-coordinates of its vertices, plot those coordinate points directly, and connect them.

reviews.scope: writing coordinates of symmetric points and plotting reflected figures in the coordinate plane
reviews.reason: Finding reflected coordinates and graphing figures symmetric across the coordinate axes directly requires reading, writing, and plotting point coordinates in the Cartesian plane.

reviews.scope: relating coordinate sign changes under reflection to quadrant positions
reviews.reason: Knowing the coordinate sign characteristics of quadrants and axes helps students check reflected coordinates and visualize how reflection across an axis moves points between quadrants.
reviews.counterexample: A student can apply the rules (a,-b) and (-a,b) directly from perpendicular distance to the coordinate axes without classifying quadrant signs.

reviews.scope: proving equal base angles and the three-line coincidence property of isosceles triangles
reviews.reason: Proving the properties of isosceles triangles is an explicit mastery criterion and requires dividing the triangle with an auxiliary segment and proving the two halves congruent.

reviews.scope: understanding the vertex angle bisector in the three-line coincidence property
reviews.reason: Stating and applying the three-line coincidence property of isosceles triangles directly requires knowing the definition of a triangle's angle bisector.

reviews.scope: understanding the median to the base in the three-line coincidence property
reviews.reason: Stating and applying the three-line coincidence property of isosceles triangles directly requires knowing the definition of a triangle's median and that it bisects the base.

reviews.scope: understanding the altitude to the base in the three-line coincidence property
reviews.reason: Stating and applying the three-line coincidence property of isosceles triangles directly requires knowing the definition of a triangle's altitude and its perpendicularity to the base.

reviews.scope: motivating the equal-angles-to-equal-sides criterion as the converse of the base-angle property
reviews.reason: Knowing the properties of isosceles triangles motivates the converse criterion, but proving and applying the criterion that equal angles imply equal opposite sides relies on AAS congruence, not isosceles properties.
reviews.counterexample: Draw the angle bisector or altitude to the side between the two equal angles and prove the two sub-triangles congruent by AAS to deduce equal sides directly.

reviews.scope: establishing and applying the angle-based criteria for equilateral triangles
reviews.reason: Showing that a triangle with three equal angles or an isosceles triangle with a 60-degree angle has all three sides equal directly relies on the isosceles triangle criterion.

reviews.scope: deriving and understanding why the leg opposite 30 degrees is half the hypotenuse
reviews.reason: In elementary synthetic geometry before trigonometry, justifying why the side opposite a 30-degree angle in a right triangle is half the hypotenuse requires constructing an equilateral triangle.

reviews.scope: reflecting a point across a line to transform a broken-line path
reviews.reason: Solving shortest-path reflection problems requires constructing a symmetric point across the given line and using reflection symmetry to equate the reflected segment lengths.

reviews.scope: justifying why the straight segment connecting the reflected point and target is shortest
reviews.reason: Explaining why the reflected straight-line path minimizes total distance is an explicit criterion and relies directly on the postulate that the line segment between two points is shortest.

reviews.scope: explaining equal distances from any point on the symmetry axis to symmetric points
reviews.reason: The perpendicular bisector property provides a clear way to justify why any point on the line is equidistant from the original point and its reflection.
reviews.counterexample: One can also justify the equal segment lengths directly from the congruence of symmetric segments under reflection without separately citing the perpendicular bisector theorem.

reviews.scope: understanding bases, exponents, and the definition of powers as repeated multiplication
reviews.reason: Deriving and applying the rule for multiplying powers with the same base requires understanding the meaning of exponents, bases, and powers as repeated multiplication.

reviews.scope: working with literal bases and distinguishing power multiplication from adding like terms
reviews.reason: Familiarity with monomials helps students work with variable powers and contrast multiplying powers with adding like terms, though the power rule itself only requires exponentiation.
reviews.counterexample: The rule a^m * a^n = a^(m+n) can be derived and applied directly from the definition of exponentiation on numbers and variables without monomial degree or coefficient concepts.

reviews.scope: deriving the power-of-a-power rule and distinguishing the three power operations
reviews.reason: Deriving the power-of-a-power rule uses repeated multiplication of same-base powers, and the criteria explicitly require distinguishing same-base power multiplication from the new power rules.

reviews.scope: multiplying powers of identical variables when multiplying monomials
reviews.reason: Multiplying two monomials requires multiplying powers of the same variable by adding their exponents, which is the same-base power multiplication rule.

reviews.scope: multiplying the monomial factor by each individual term of the polynomial
reviews.reason: Applying the distributive law to multiply a monomial by a polynomial requires multiplying the monomial by each monomial term of the polynomial.

reviews.scope: simplifying expressions when multiple monomial-by-polynomial products are added
reviews.reason: Multiplying a single monomial by a simplified polynomial produces terms with distinct variable parts, so combining like terms is only needed in extended multi-product simplification exercises.
reviews.counterexample: Expanding a single monomial-by-polynomial product such as 2x(3x^2 - 4x + 5) = 6x^3 - 8x^2 + 10x requires only the distributive law and monomial multiplication, with no like terms to combine.

reviews.scope: distributing each term of one polynomial across the other polynomial
reviews.reason: Multiplying two polynomials is performed by distributing each monomial term of the first polynomial over the second polynomial, directly applying monomial-by-polynomial multiplication.

reviews.scope: understanding and deriving the binomial product (a+b)(a-b) = a^2 - b^2
reviews.reason: The difference of squares formula is a specialized shortcut for multiplying two binomials, requiring polynomial multiplication to understand the expression and why the cross terms cancel.

reviews.scope: interpreting the perfect square formula geometrically via square and rectangle areas
reviews.reason: Decomposing a square of side (a+b) into smaller squares and rectangles provides an intuitive geometric explanation of the formula alongside its algebraic derivation.
reviews.counterexample: The formula (a+b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2 can be derived and applied purely algebraically by expanding (a+b)(a+b) via polynomial multiplication without area models.

reviews.scope: expanding (a+b)(a+b) and (a-b)(a-b) to understand the middle 2ab term
reviews.reason: The perfect square formula is a special case of multiplying two identical binomials, requiring polynomial multiplication to derive the expansion and understand the middle 2ab term.

reviews.scope: comparing the perfect square formula with the difference of squares formula
reviews.reason: Both formulas are independent special cases of binomial multiplication with no required learning order between them, though contrasting them helps avoid omitting the middle term.
reviews.counterexample: A student can derive and master (a+b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2 directly from polynomial multiplication before or without studying the difference of squares formula.

reviews.scope: applying the difference of squares formula in combined polynomial simplifications
reviews.reason: Combined application of multiplication formulas explicitly requires recognizing and applying the difference of squares formula within multi-step algebraic expansions.

reviews.scope: applying the perfect square formula in combined polynomial simplifications
reviews.reason: Combined application of multiplication formulas explicitly requires applying the perfect square formula, including after grouping terms by inserting parentheses.

reviews.scope: inserting parentheses for substitution and removing parentheses in mixed polynomial operations
reviews.reason: Grouping terms by inserting parentheses and simplifying mixed products with subtraction directly rely on the sign rules for removing and inserting parentheses.

reviews.scope: understanding factorization as the inverse operation of polynomial multiplication
reviews.reason: The concept of factorization is defined as rewriting a polynomial as a product of polynomials, and the criteria explicitly require explaining its inverse relation to polynomial multiplication.

reviews.scope: understanding the goal and target product form of factoring out a common factor
reviews.reason: Factoring out a common factor is a method of polynomial factorization, requiring knowledge of what factorization means and that the result must be a product of polynomials.

reviews.scope: understanding polynomial factorization and complete factored form
reviews.reason: Factoring polynomials via the difference of squares requires understanding the concept of factorization as rewriting a sum into an irreducible product of polynomials.

reviews.scope: reversing the difference of squares identity to factor polynomials
reviews.reason: Factoring a difference of two squares directly applies the difference of squares multiplication identity in reverse.

reviews.scope: understanding polynomial factorization when rewriting a trinomial as a squared binomial
reviews.reason: Factoring perfect square trinomials requires understanding the concept of polynomial factorization and its goal of expressing a polynomial as a product.

reviews.scope: recognizing perfect square trinomials and reversing the perfect square identity
reviews.reason: Identifying a perfect square trinomial and factoring it into a squared binomial directly reverses the perfect square multiplication formula.

reviews.scope: extracting common factors as the first step in multi-step factorization
reviews.reason: Combined factorization explicitly requires factoring out the greatest common factor first before applying formula methods to achieve complete factorization.

reviews.scope: applying the difference of squares method in multi-step factorization
reviews.reason: Combined factorization explicitly requires applying formula methods such as the difference of squares after extracting common factors until no factor can be reduced further.

reviews.scope: applying the perfect square formula method in multi-step factorization
reviews.reason: Combined factorization explicitly requires applying formula methods such as the perfect square trinomial method after extracting common factors to factor completely.
